content.title: The First Generation: When Faith Began Without Power
paragraphs: Chapter Six
The First Generation: When Faith Began Without Power

In the previous chapter, the call began as a small circle around the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. There was no mosque in Makkah filled with thousands of Muslims, no state to protect them, and no social majority that made accepting Islam easy. Each person heard the message and then chose whether to believe, knowing that he or she was entering a road whose future was still unknown.

In the books of Seerah, these people are often described as the first generation or the early forerunners: the first group to enter the path before others. The Qur’an itself gave special value to being first and later described a group of the Companions in these words:

As for the first forerunners of the Emigrants and the Helpers, and those who followed them in righteous deeds, Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him. He has prepared for them gardens under which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the supreme triumph.
Qur’an 9:100 — Rowwad Translation Center (QuranEnc)

The Emigrants were the Muslims who would later leave Makkah for the sake of their faith, while the Helpers were the Muslims of Madinah who would welcome the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and support him. This verse was revealed years after the period we are reading about now, but it helps explain why Islam preserved a special place for those who came forward when support was scarce and the road was difficult.

Being early, therefore, was not simply a ranking of names: who accepted Islam first and who came next. It meant believing in the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, when there was no army, no state, and no visible victory around him. The stranger and weaker Islam appeared at the beginning, the more truthfulness and courage it took to join it.

The first picture of this small community appeared inside the Prophet’s own home. Khadijah, may Allah be pleased with her, believed in him and affirmed the truth of his message from the beginning of revelation; she was his wife and had known his life and honesty for years before prophethood. ‘Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, was among the earliest believers and was then a young boy living in the Prophet’s home. Zayd ibn Harithah, may Allah be pleased with him, was also among the earliest believers; he had once been enslaved, then the Prophet freed him before the mission, and he remained close to him.

Then there was Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, a free man well known among Quraysh and a well-connected merchant of standing. Abu Bakr did not stop at believing by himself. He began speaking to people he knew and trusted, and through his invitation several men entered Islam who would later become among the best-known Companions: ‘Uthman ibn ‘Affan, al-Zubayr ibn al-‘Awwam, ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn ‘Awf, Sa‘d ibn Abi Waqqas, and Talhah ibn ‘Ubaydillah, may Allah be pleased with them.

The sources differ about the order in which some people accepted Islam after the earliest believers. Yet a community was taking shape: a household, then a friend, then the friend of a friend, until a small group of believers had gathered around the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. They knew one another and were united in worshipping Allah alone and following His Messenger.

An authentic report shows just how small this number appeared in one early moment. A man named ‘Amr ibn ‘Abasah, may Allah be pleased with him, came to Makkah after hearing news of the Prophet. He found the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, living cautiously because his people had begun treating him harshly. ‘Amr asked about his message, and the Prophet told him that Allah had sent him to maintain family ties, break the idols, and worship Allah alone without associating anything with Him.

‘Amr asked, “Who is with you in this (in these beliefs and practices)?” The Prophet replied, “A free man and a slave.” The narrator said that Abu Bakr and Bilal were with him among those who had embraced Islam by that time.
Sahih Muslim 832 — excerpts from the published English translation on Sunnah.com.

Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, represented a free man with status among his people, while Bilal ibn Rabah, may Allah be pleased with him, was an enslaved man in Makkah. Seeing them together in this early picture matters: the message did not begin as the religion of one social class. From the beginning it included the wealthy and the poor, the free and the enslaved, men and women, adults and young people.

Here, ‘enslaved person’ means someone living under the system of slavery known in that world, belonging legally to a master and not possessing full freedom over his or her life. A person who was freed was sometimes called a mawla — here meaning a former slave who had been emancipated while retaining a recognized social bond of loyalty with the person who freed him. These differences would soon become very important, because someone protected by a strong tribe was not in the same position as someone who had no clan able to stop others from torturing him.

Women were present from the very beginning as well; their story was not a side note to the story of the men. Khadijah, may Allah be pleased with her, was the first to believe the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and support him in his home. Among the women who accepted Islam early was Umm al-Fadl Lubabah bint al-Harith, may Allah be pleased with her, the wife of al-‘Abbas ibn ‘Abd al-Muttalib. Reports indicate that she embraced Islam before her husband and remained in Makkah during a period when the Muslims were still weak and vulnerable.

Another of the earliest believing women was Sumayyah bint Khayyat, the mother of ‘Ammar ibn Yasir, may Allah be pleased with them. She was not a powerful woman of Quraysh protected by a strong clan; she was among the vulnerable — people who lacked enough social or tribal power to protect themselves. When persecution intensified, she remained firm in Islam until she was killed. Scholars transmitted from Ibn Sa‘d, through a sound chain, that she was the first martyr in Islam. The story of what happened to the family of Yasir will come when the narrative reaches Quraysh’s torture of the Muslims.

There were also very young believers in this generation. ‘Ali’s presence at the beginning reminds us that faith was not a decision made only by older people. Biographical works, including collections arranged by generation, mention a number of Companions who were very young when they entered Islam and later lived through Badr, Uhud, the Hijrah, and the other great events of the Seerah. At that moment they were not yet the famous names we know today; they were young people choosing to connect their future to a message that was still at its beginning.

This was the meaning of being early that would remain remembered even after the Muslim community grew much larger. Years later, a minor disagreement occurred between Abu Bakr and ‘Umar, may Allah be pleased with them, and the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, reminded the Companions of how Abu Bakr had stood beside him at the beginning. He said:

“Certainly, Allah sent me to you all and you all said I was lying whereas Abu Bakr affirmed my truthfulness and further supported me with his life and wealth. Will you not spare my companion for my sake?”

Sahih al-Bukhari 3661 — excerpt from the English translation published by Mahajjah, Sayyidina Abu Bakr al Siddiq – The Companion in the Cave and the Comrade on Journeys, “Al Siddiq: a Magnificent Support in Adversity”.

The meaning was not that the other Companions had no virtue. Rather, beginnings carry a cost that can be invisible to people who arrive after the road has become wider. Allah expresses a similar principle regarding spending and fighting before the Muslims became stronger:

Why is it that you do not spend in the cause of Allah, when Allah alone will inherit the heavens and earth? Those of you who spent and fought before the conquest [of Makkah and those who did not] are not equal. They are much greater in rank than those who spent and fought afterward. Yet Allah has promised each a fine reward, and Allah is All-Aware of what you do.
Qur’an 57:10 — Rowwad Translation Center (QuranEnc)

This verse was revealed at a later stage, and Qur’anic commentators differed over exactly which ‘victory’ is meant. The point relevant here is clear: the same deed can carry greater weight when it is done at a time when support costs more and those standing with the truth are fewer.

In the early years in Makkah, simply announcing that a person followed Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, could change relationships with family, tribe, or master. Some believers had families that could protect them; others had no such protection. Some were wealthy and could control their own property; others were enslaved and could not simply leave their owner’s house whenever they wished. Yet faith brought them together into one community.

They learned the Qur’an as it was revealed and worshipped Allah according to what He had prescribed for them in that period. Prayer was among the earliest acts of worship in Islam, but the five daily prayers would become obligatory later, on the night of the Night Journey and Ascension (Sahih al-Bukhari 349, 350). The reports concerning the details of worship at this earliest stage vary in strength, so not every detail can be established with the same degree of certainty.

Islam in Makkah therefore began not as a huge crowd, but as a small number of names. Some came from the Prophet’s household, some were prominent members of Quraysh, some were young, some were enslaved or socially vulnerable, and women had entered the path from its very beginning. They were not united by one lineage or one social class; what united them was that they believed the message before they had seen its worldly results.

As this small number grew, it became harder for their existence to go unnoticed by Quraysh. A call that had begun inside homes and in individual meetings was becoming more visible. Makkah would begin to realize that this was not merely a private religious choice made by a few people, but a message that touched the idols, inherited customs, and the authority of what their forefathers had passed down.

From here the nature of the story changes. The question is no longer only, ‘Who believed?’ It becomes: what will Quraysh do when they realize that this call is continuing and that the number of its believers is growing?
Main sources

Sources: Qur’an 9:100 and 57:10; Sahih Muslim 832; Sahih al-Bukhari 3661; Ibn Hisham’s Seerah from Ibn Ishaq; Ibn Sa‘d’s al-Tabaqat al-Kubra; al-Dhahabi’s Siyar A‘lam al-Nubala’. The reported order of some early converts differs between sources. On Sumayyah, may Allah be pleased with her, as the first martyr in Islam: Ibn Hajar, al-Isabah, her biographical entry, citing Ibn Sa‘d’s report from Mujahid with a chain he grades as sound.
